item.title: The port-call situation is wearing out Navy warships
item.description: Diego Garcia is the only safe place for ships fighting Iran, but the remote atoll can’t provide the maintenance they need.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Hlad
item.content:encoded:
A few years ago, a port call in the Middle East might mean bottomless-mojito brunches in Bahrain, hitting the indoor ski slopes in a Dubai megamall, or a desert safari in Qatar. But since Operation Epic Fury began eight months ago, U.S. warships in the theater have basically had just one option: Diego Garcia, some 2,500 miles away.

It’s not great for morale, but the consequences go beyond disgruntled sailors who tire of fishing off the British island in the Indian Ocean. The remote coral atoll lacks the pierside infrastructure that many Gulf, Mediterranean, and Pacific ports can offer. As the Navy stretches its fleet with longer deployments and fewer port calls, warships are losing the ability to do crucial mid-cruise maintenance.

“When a ship is deployed overseas for longer than the nominal seven-month deployment period, that increases the amount of time for equipment on the ship to break, get worn down, or worn out. As a result, when the ship finally does make it back to the United States, it might need more maintenance and repair work than it would have needed if the deployment had not exceeded seven months,” said Ron O’Rourke, who retired this year after more than 40 years as a naval analyst for the Congressional Research Service.

“That can increase the time and cost to do the maintenance and repair work, and an increased time needed to do the work could prevent other ships from entering maintenance and overhaul as scheduled. This can lead to a cascading effect in delaying maintenance on other ships.”

A Navy officer with expertise in maritime security agreed, noting that “even deployed ships need time alongside”—that is, moored directly to a pier or tender vessel for what’s called voyage repair availability—“to fix broken things, remediate rust, paint, etc. If these ships are kept out for 10 to 12 months, they’ll be missing other scheduled maintenance events and be much more broken than they should be when they get home.”

The Navy itself nodded to the problem in a recent press release about the aircraft carrier Abraham Lincoln, which is changing homeports to receive overdue depot-level maintenance after a nearly 11-month deployment.

“Regularly scheduled depot-level maintenance maximizes the lifespan of our Navy vessels and keeps our fleets lethal, modern, and ready to defend the nation.”

[[Related Posts]]

The Lincoln’s 321-day deployment—and the carrier Gerald R. Ford’s 326-day deployment before it—set records for consecutive days at sea and length of deployment, respectively. But a few Arleigh Burke-class guided missile destroyers are on track to far surpass those numbers. And Navy officials recently told families in Yokosuka, Japan, that for the foreseeable future they should expect all ships to deploy for 10 to 12 months.

A Navy spokesperson said they would “not discuss specific readiness rates, operational requirements, force-allocation deliberations, or future force movements. However, we remain committed to regular maintenance to maximize the lifespan of our Navy vessels and keep our fleets lethal and ready to defend our nation.”

‘It’s empty’

Instead of the luxury hotels and hundreds of restaurants sailors can visit in ports like Dubai and Bahrain, Diego Garcia has a military supply base and a small town with a handful of restaurants. And since virtually every ship deployed in the region is using the island for port calls and resupply, store shelves don’t always stay stocked.

The guided-missile destroyer John Finn, which left Japan in January, pulled into Diego Garcia after months at sea.

“Everybody’s going to the ship store and it’s empty,” a sailor’s spouse told Defense One. “You can find ice cream, but you’re not going to find your necessities that you need to function.”

The ship had pulled in because it was “empty,” the spouse said, after having spent all of its weapons in the campaign against Iran. “So they had to spend that week resupplying.”

The spouse of a sailor on the Mustin, another guided-missile destroyer, said her husband was able to get socks but not shoe polish at the exchange on base during the only port call the ship has made since leaving Japan in April.

“He got off like, preparing to be able to get the stuff that he needed right now, and he goes, ‘They don’t have shit,’” she said. “They didn’t have anything.”

For the Mustin crew, the port call seemed like a welcome respite from their months at sea, until they were told just before getting off the ship that they would not return in August as originally planned, but stay deployed until April 2027, the spouse told Defense One.

“The sad part is, they were actually in good spirits,” she said. “And then I know things went really rowdy in Diego Garcia because they were given the bad news literally the day before they pulled in. … There was one of the nights in Diego Garcia that two sailors ended up in the ER with alcohol poisoning. And so then they lost their last night of liberty because of it.”

O’Rourke said the British island “can provide an opportunity to be on land for a while, and to engage in certain R&R activities. But the options for doing R&R things at Diego Garcia are a lot more limited than they are at other ports, such as Singapore or somewhere in the Mediterranean.” 

Ralph Cossa, chairman of the Pacific Forum, was less diplomatic.

“Please shoot me if that’s the only R&R I’m going to get in 10 months,” he said.

Mail delays

Sailors have asked their families and friends to send them supplies, but mail is taking three to six months to reach the destroyers, the spouses said.

The Mustin spouse sent her husband several boxes at the start of the summer; all but one took four months to arrive. The John Finn spouse said it also took four months for a few packages to reach her sailor, and some that “took even longer than six months to get out there.”

“I think I’ve sent my husband the same thing three different times now, and I’m like, well, hopefully one of these gets to you in the next two or three months, and whenever the other ones show up, you’re just gonna have an abundance. Share it with somebody else.”

Both spouses expressed concern about the sailors’ ability to vote in the upcoming elections, given the mail delays. The John Finn spouse said her husband, who has done multiple deployments in the past, said, “There has been no conversation about voting because we don’t have time for it. We don’t have time to even have conversations because we are busy doing all of this other crap that nobody wants to be doing to begin with.”

By contrast, sailors aboard the George Washington aircraft carrier generally “can expect to receive mail shipped from the states within weeks,” Lt. Cmdr. Bobby Dixon, a ship spokesperson, told Defense One. “However, this can take longer when deployed overseas. We work with our U.S. military logistics teammates to minimize mail delays and we are committed to ensuring all service members can exercise their right to vote.”

Maintenance

Navy ships, like any other vehicles, require a certain amount of maintenance to continue working. There are three levels of repairs: basic, intermediate, and depot-level maintenance. 

Deployed ships are under stress from the salt water and sea air, and more things are likely to wear down or break when they’re being used frequently for long periods of time. And the forward-deployed destroyers based in Yokosuka—including the John Finn and the Mustin—are usually in a cycle in which they spend just a few months at sea before heading back home for a few months of maintenance.

Now those two destroyers are slated to be at sea for a year or more, which will mean they will miss the beginning of their planned five-month shipyard maintenance periods. And the Mustin spouse said there were already some maintenance problems on that ship when it shifted homeports from San Diego, Calif., to Yokosuka, just before it left for deployment.

“Their maintenance log was 100 percent not empty,” and there were a lot of things “that they should have been turned around for,” she said. The ship was told to head to Japan anyway. 

And though the sailors were told their lone port call was planned so they could perform maintenance, “they never got anything fixed when they went to Diego Garcia. … They didn’t actually go up pierside.”

O’Rourke said there are consequences for delays to the intermediate and depot levels of maintenance.

“If you have a period where the total fraction of the Navy being on deployment overseas is elevated above what the notional model calls for, there will be a period downstream where you have to pay the piper, where the fraction of the Navy that will be available for deployment will be less than what the notional model called for because you're making up for that earlier period,” he said.

It’s not a new problem.

“Years ago, the Navy got itself into a hole on conventional surface ship maintenance due in part to what turned out to be underestimates in planning, scheduling, and funding that work. Since then, the Navy has been working for years to dig itself out of that conventional surface ship maintenance hole. Perturbations in ship maintenance and repair schedules caused by ships being used for extended deployments can add to the Navy’s challenge of digging itself out of that hole,” O’Rourke said.

So the service needs to give its ships the maintenance they need. But that’s unlikely to happen while the Navy is keeping so many ships in theater, a second Navy expert said.

“The end result is that deferred maintenance becomes more and more problematic, causing knock-on effects like parts and equipment wearing out or breaking before they should. In the end, these ships will reach their end of service life well before their scheduled date.”

item.title: Financial aid for Ukraine is getting harder to find
item.description: Helping a European neighbor remains politically popular, but rearming amid economic stress leaves less money to give.
item.dc:creator: Derek Bisaccio, Forecast International
item.content:encoded:
European leaders meet next month to discuss ways to help Ukraine fill a projected €70 billion budget deficit. But their capacity for direct aid is constrained by efforts to rearm their own militaries amid a challenging economic environment, while Belgium continues to oppose the conversion of frozen Russian assets into a loan. 

Western financial aid—€170 billion ($189.5 billion) since 2022—has been key to helping Kyiv stay financially afloat since Russia's wider invasion, according to the Kiel Institute. But the U.S. has drastically cut aid under the second Trump administration, leaving the European Union, Canada, Japan, Norway, and the United Kingdom to shoulder most of the burden. 

Earlier this year, the EU approved a plan to lend Ukraine €90 billion to Ukraine through 2027, two-thirds of which will go to buy weapons and the rest to budgetary support. Around €14 billion has been disbursed to date, and by year's end that figure should grow to €45 billion.

But Russian attacks on critical infrastructure and other stresses mean that Kyiv is still looking at a budget deficit of around €70 billion for 2027. 

European governments are spending more on their own defenses. In 2021, the defense budgets of NATO's European members averaged around 1.6 percent of GDP, below NATO’s then-target of 2 percent. The alliance has since boosted its goal to 2.5 percent of GDP, and at last year's summit, committed to raising ‘core’ defense expenditure to 3.5 percent  over the next decade.

At the same time, they are facing rising debt and slowing economies. Eurozone countries have an average debt-to-GDP ratio of nearly 89 percent, and nearly 83 percent in EU nations generally. Buffeted by the trade wars and energy shocks of the Trump administration, eurozone economies will grow only 1.1 percent in 2026, according to a recent projection by the International Monetary Fund. Some northern EU members are in much better fiscal shape than their southern and western counterparts.

The budget picture is getting cloudier. Annual inflation in the eurozone rose to 3.8 percent in September, according to Eurostat, well above the European Central Bank (ECB) target of 2 percent. The ECB raised interest rates at its June and September meetings, and is expected to deliver another hike at one of the year's two remaining meetings. Rising prices may force the ECB to continue tightening policy, raising debt-service payments from government budgets. 

Supporting Ukraine remains broadly popular in the EU, but the challenging economic environment makes it a tough sell for governments to increase aid to Ukraine along with their own defense spending. European governments are already facing domestic criticism over rearmament. Italy, for example, was approved for an allocation of up to €14.9 billion from the E.U.’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) loan facility, meant to aid rearmament. Yet Rome requested only about €8 billion from SAFE, as Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government sparred with critics within her own coalition and in the opposition on financing more defense spending with debt. 

Frozen Russian assets

EU countries are thus once again looking at alternative methods of backstopping Ukraine’s budget. One of the most obvious options is the conversion of frozen Russian financial assets into a loan to Kyiv. 

After Russia's February 2022 invasion, the G7 froze Russian government securities held abroad. As much as $300 billion was impounded as a result and remains in limbo to this day, including about €210 billion held in the European financial system. 

While the principal has remained untouched, the EU has begun to use the interest income on those securities to help Ukraine, on the grounds that Russia, as aggressor, should pay for the damage caused to Ukraine. That has generated about €8 billion, of which €3.8 billion has been delivered to Ukraine, and €4.2 billion has been reserved to repay E.U. or G7 loans to Ukraine. 

In September, Germany and other E.U. members revived the topic of converting the Russian assets into a loan for Kyiv, POLITICO reported. Berlin views the step as a ‘win-win’ for the E.U., enabling the bloc to help Kyiv address its financial needs, while replacing some of the funds that would be reserved for Ukraine in the E.U.’s upcoming multi-year budget. 

But the politics around seizing the Russian assets have barely budged. 

Belgium is the custodian of much of those Russian funds, which are housed in the Brussels-based Euroclear. The Belgian government blocked a 2025 proposal to seize the funds, fearing that it alone would bear the legal and financial risk of seizing the funds. Earlier this year, the Bank of Russia sued Euroclear in a Russian court for the funds, arguing that they were illegally seized. The court backed the Russian central bank’s challenge in a ruling two months later, though it lacks jurisdiction to enforce the judgment. 

Concern over the legal risks means Brussels will likely stymie the proposal again. 

“I am certain that the European Commission will not make proposals to meet Ukraine’s financing needs through a new operation linked to Russian assets,” Belgian Prime Minister Bart de Wever told reporters on Oct. 21. “I am certain of that, because that is what was said.” 

As European leaders prepare for a November meeting to iron out next year's assistance to Ukraine, the EU is already pushing other partners to increase their contributions to Kyiv. 

The situation is becoming more urgent. Ukraine has largely exhausted its stockpile of interceptors, leaving its cities and energy grid vulnerable to Russian attack. The Ukrainian military intelligence agency HUR recently estimated that Russia can produce 10,000 long-range strike drones and decoys each month. Mounting damage increases Ukraine’s financial needs, as the country scrambles to keep the lights on.

item.title: The Army’s only remaining SFAB helped broker a ceasefire in southeast Asia
item.description: The service’s last train-advise-assist unit is working to counter Chinese influence in the Indo-Pacific theater.
item.dc:creator: Meghann Myers
item.content:encoded:
A year ago, after months of fighting spurred by a century-old border dispute, Thailand and Cambodia struck a peace deal in Malaysia, with help from a small U.S. Army unit that had long been training both Thai and Malaysian troops.

The peace talks were led by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and the Malaysian Land Forces, which sought the advice of the 5th Security Force Assistance Brigade, the unit’s commander told Defense One.

“They asked our advisors, who were in the space of the land force headquarters, ‘Hey, what should we be thinking about? How can we effectively do this?,” said Col. Daniel Hodermarsky. “And we were reporting back to [U.S. Army Pacific] and leveraging experts from the higher headquarters to provide that advice to more rapidly enable them to to take the lead.”

At the same time, 5th SFAB had a team on the ground in Thailand.

“We didn't have anyone near the front or in the conflict, but we were able to say, "Hey, here's what we're seeing with the country team in Thailand,” Hodermarsky said.

But 5th SFAB—the Army’s only remaining train-advise-assist unit—didn’t just happen to be in the right place at the right time. The specialized unit, made up of experienced conventional troops who have already led a squad or platoon, and so on, has been regularly deploying to INDOPACOM to work with partner militaries since 2020.

“So we're able to give a bit more granular, real-time reporting back to the theater, and we're tied in directly with each country team, security cooperation office and defense attaché wherever we have adviser teams,” Hodermarsky said. “So we can get those liaise cells, those assessment cells, and say, ‘Hey, here's what we're granularly seeing, hearing. Here's what the partner is asking, or here's what they're talking about.”

The Army developed the SFAB concept in 2017, when training and advising the Afghan army had no end in sight and the service was anticipating expanding that mission beyond U.S. Central Command. The idea was that rather than rotating conventional infantry and other units as advisers, the service would cultivate specialized units for the mission. The 1st SFAB deployed in Afghanistan in 2018.

By May 2020, six SFABs had been established, each aligned to a different part of the world. They were staffed by volunteers coming off operational assignments, now experienced and theoretically qualified to train a partner unit.

Last year, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ordered most of the SFABs to be dissolved. The units assigned to European and Africa Commands have been shuttered, and their CENTCOM and National Guard counterparts will be gone by year’s end. 1st SFAB was reorganized as Army Security Cooperation Group-South in January. 

That leaves only Hodermarsky’s 5th, doing its part to keep the United States in the good graces of INDOPACOM countries that might otherwise align themselves with China’s growing military power. 

Some have argued that the moves are shortsighted.

“If the U.S. military continues marginalizing the advising mission or ignoring it altogether, then it means going back to the failed train-and-pray model,” argued a 2025 piece published by West Point’s Modern War Institute. “Fully staffed SFABs are not a luxury; they’re a necessity. Without them, the United States risks being flat-footed in the next war.” 

ASCG-S and 5th SFAB’s continued existence are an acknowledgement that the train-advise-assist mission is still important for the DOD’s top two priority regions.

5th’s farflung efforts

In INDOPACOM, 5th SFAB has been shaping militaries from Mongolia to the Philippines, embedding in their professional military academies as well as advising their senior leadership.

“We were in the Philippine Army headquarters and their [Training and Doctrine Command] equivalent for years, as they transitioned from a counterinsurgency focus across the Philippines, to a national-defense focus for their land forces” Hodermarsky said.

His unit’s relationships have also laid the groundwork for major exercises the Army now does in INDOPACOM, including Balikatan and Cobra Gold. 

“A persistent advisor team can stay in between the planning conferences and come up with the training plan, if we identify the partner unit that's going to exercise with the 25th Infantry Division or the the 7th Infantry Division,” Hodermarsky said. “And say, what are the training objectives for that Royal Thai Army unit or Philippine Army unit or Malaysian Land Force element? And then help them through that training progression.”

He said some division leaders call the SFAB the WD-40 of U.S. Army Pacific, because their teams ease friction between partner nations and conventional units visiting for exercises.

“We see sort of a reverse slope of advisor presence, as we hopefully work our way out of jobs in certain countries, so that you go from a partner force requesting more hands-on training and capability development through security force assistance, to where they're now really exercising as a flank unit or an integrated part of a U.S. division or brigade that is more capable, more trusted to be on our flank, or integrated into one of our major formations,” Hodermarsky said.

item.title: At last, Army seeing progress in Pacific network
item.description: Recent exercises suggest the service and its foreign partners are moving closer to a single-screen data system.
item.dc:creator: Lauren C. Williams
item.content:encoded:
WASHINGTON—After years of frustration, Army leaders are starting to see progress on upgraded networks designed to make it easier to communicate with allies and partners in a Pacific conflict. 

“When I arrived at [U.S. Army Pacific Command], we had an exercise in Japan—and I'd only been in command a month. It was a trilateral exercise between the U.S., Japan, and Australia. And we literally couldn't pass voice data to each other. We couldn't create a common operating picture without physically putting icons into this system,” Gen. Ronald Clark, commander of U.S. Army Pacific, told reporters earlier this month. 

“It was so frustrating to me because I just left working in the Pentagon where I had literally attended both the signing ceremonies for AUKUS…sharing our most sensitive defense technology. But we are using basically a swivel chair to have a conversation with regard to land forces.”

In recent years, the Army has been building and testing the telecommunications pipelines that allies and partner militaries would rely on in a war with China. U.S. Indo-Pacific Command has a broader Pacific Mission Network, previously known as the INDOPACOM Mission Network, which is used on a more strategic or operational level. 

Earlier this year, the U.S., Australia, and Japan used the Pacific Mission Network during the large Balikatan exercise to get a “real-time picture of participating forces across the entire training area,” an Army spokesperson told Defense One.

Months later, the nations reconvened for Yama Sakura 91, an annual military exercise with Japan and Australia that ended Sept. 10.

“Yama Sakura 91 demonstrated the live sharing of simulated information in a command post exercise, while Balikatan 26 demonstrated the live sharing of real-time information across a physical training environment and multiple echelons,” the Army said.

That network, which connects dozens of nations, was the linchpin for USARPAC to test whether it could share and see the same information as allies and partners.

“The [mission partner] enclaves work, so we're able to pass and share data in a way that we had not been before,” Clark said, at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference, calling the network an “important and critical innovation” that addressed years of frustrations. 

That means commanders can more easily send “target-quality data” and share a “common operational picture” without needing to swivel between workstations.

For example, Maj. Gen. Bernard Harrington, who leads the Army’s Multi-Domain Command-Pacific and 7th Infantry Division, can gather information on “land-based long-range precision fires, sensors, space capability, [electronic warfare], cyber” and then share it with Pacific Fleet Commander Adm. Stephen Koehler, who led the exercise, and “can then integrate that [data] into a joint context in the fight,” Clark said.

The progress on the Pacific Mission Network comes as the Army looks to add more tech and sources of data—mostly drones—to its forces. That means being able to see, control, and learn from devices and the information they collect will become increasingly important on the battlefield. 

Seventh ID recently finished an exercise called Bayonet Quest near Lake Huron, Mich., in which it was able to coordinate high-altitude balloons, and aerial and maritime drones, using a shared data connection, Harrington told reporters. 

“We used multiple [unmanned aerial systems], multiple [unmanned surface vessels], long-range, one-way attack, and a high-altitude balloon,” he said. The division also collected and analyzed data from all of those systems using a single data layer. 

During the exercise, which ended Oct. 6, the Army was also able to orchestrate the drones and coordinate simulated attacks with an “adaptive and agentic” command-and-control system. 

“We were able to pull in a vast amount of data, make sense of it quickly, and then task those systems through a large language model, reducing the need for soldiers on individual ground control stations,” Harrington said in a statement to Defense One.

The exercise showed how unmanned systems could be used in the Pacific, particularly from different locations, which could help keep soldiers safe, he said.

The exercise wrapped earlier this month, but the division plans to keep training with the concept and employ it in future exercises with allies and partners.

item.title: Policy proposal would require firms to disclose how they use AI to develop new models
item.description: The framework from Americans for Responsible Innovation would give Washington a closer look at AI’s role in developing new models as Jay Clayton’s task force shapes the government’s relationship with developers.
item.dc:creator: David DiMolfetta
item.content:encoded:
Artificial intelligence companies would have to report how they use their own technology to build new AI models under a proposal aimed at helping Washington track AI advances and whether developers are adequately testing their safety.

The plan, developed by Americans for Responsible Innovation and shared first with Nextgov/FCW, would require major developers to submit quarterly reports to a new Commerce Department office and disclose significant research changes within four business days. The group, which advocates for federal AI oversight, wants officials to know how much research AI is performing and how closely people are supervising it.

The proposal arrives as the White House deepens its involvement with AI companies while resisting calls for a broad new regulatory regime. President Donald Trump this month tapped Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to lead the “Super Intelligence Force,” a task force coordinating government engagement with developers and other groups and assessing the technology’s risks. The executive order creating the group was signed late last month.

Clayton’s group is already working on how companies alert the government when something goes wrong. Following its first formal meeting, it assigned Pentagon technology official Emil Michael to develop protocols for labs to report breaches, hacks and other cyber issues. It also commissioned a study of risks involving cybersecurity, biological threats and control of AI systems.

ARI wants companies to report when AI takes on more of the work of building new models, even if nothing goes wrong. The group argues that automating research could speed up development and leave officials with less time to assess the risks of increasingly powerful systems.

“Washington’s visibility into that shift should not depend on what companies choose to announce,” a blog post for the framework says.

AI system development involves writing code, preparing data to train the models, running tests and deciding which results warrant further work. Automating more of those tasks could help companies produce more capable systems faster, but safety researchers and officials may have less time to assess those systems before they are put to use.

Recent cybersecurity episodes have shown what increasingly capable AI systems can do. This past week, researchers used AI to uncover critical weaknesses in PHP, software that helps run websites worldwide, prompting urgent warnings from U.S. cybersecurity agencies. 

ARI’s blog also cites a landmark AI-cyber intrusion earlier this year in which an OpenAI agent escaped its testing environment and breached Hugging Face. The incident was soon followed by disclosures of AI agents that targeted federal systems.

Such hacking capabilities are among the risks ARI wants developers required to assess. Its proposed standards would also cover large-scale influence operations and chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear and explosive threats. 

A major change, such as fully automating a research cycle, could trigger the four-day notification requirement, the proposal says. Commerce could ask follow-up questions, require more frequent reporting and refer knowingly false or incomplete filings to the Justice Department. The framework also calls for a whistleblower program.

Commerce already evaluates advanced models through a NIST center that works with developers under voluntary agreements to assess risks, including hacking capabilities. The blueprint would draw on technical analysis from the existing hub — known as the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence — to shape safety standards and determine which models fall under federal oversight. 

It leaves open whether regulatory responsibilities would sit within Commerce or be shared across agencies. 

Nextgov/FCW has asked the Commerce Department for comment on the proposal.

The administration has so far emphasized company-led safeguards, including a September accord signed by major technology executives that calls for internal controls, outside audits and independent oversight committees. Clayton’s task force is working to implement that agreement.

Earlier this month, Sens. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., and Mike Rounds, R-S.D., urged Clayton and White House science adviser Michael Kratsios to expand independent testing and strengthen protections against AI systems acting beyond their permissions.

item.title: Funding, force-structure issues could hinder Hegseth’s new autonomous command
item.description: The money to start AUTOWARCOM is to come from a reconciliation bill whose passage is in doubt.
item.dc:creator: Meghann Myers
item.content:encoded:
The Pentagon’s effort to launch a new combatant command for autonomous warfare depends on an unusual funding bill whose passage is far from assured. And while Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has given his department a full year to start up U.S. Autonomous Warfare Command, the Pentagon has little of the relevant force structure that earlier functional COCOMs could draw on.

“They have no idea. They don't know, nor should they. There's nobody on that stage that actually knows how to build anything like this,” John G. Ferrari, a nonresident senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and retired two-star general, told Defense One.

Ferrari was referring to an Oct. 14 panel featuring Hegseth, the service secretaries, and the Pentagon’s top special operations civilian. 

“But they've now set the direction and the intent,” he said. “And they're going to give it to a commander and say, ‘Now go build it.’ ”

Hegseth sat down to discuss the new command on the final day of the AUSA annual meeting in Washington, D.C., moderated by Owen West, the first CEO of the new Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems. The secretary said AUTOWARCOM would become the Pentagon’s official purchaser of autonomous technology, but offered few other details.

“My vision for AUTOWARCOM, in two years, is that we're still iterating, we're still adapting, we're still learning, and we're moving faster and faster because we're doing it,” he said. “We understand how to do it better with each iteration.”

West later ribbed Hegseth, saying that he counted the secretary saying “iteration” and “adaptation” seven times during an answer to one question. Indeed, most of the Pentagon’s messaging about AUTOWARCOM has included what they want to do, and less how they are going to do it.

Needed: force structure

Though U.S. Autonomous Warfare Command would be a functional combatant command like Cyber Command and Special Operations Command before it, in many ways it will be working backwards rather than building upon existing force structure. The plan calls for creating service component commands where there were none; and creating a new autonomous-warfare corps of officers and enlisted service members. Neither Hegseth’s memo directing the creation of the command nor the more recently released “operational roadmap" describe how these specialties will integrate with existing units.

A four-star combatant command whose primary mission is acquisitions doesn’t make a whole lot of sense, according to Mark Cancian, a senior adviser at the Center for Security and International Studies. 

“Typically, [COCOMs] operate forces. So having one that just does acquisition requires a wide variety of new authorities on acquisition, which they might be able to get,” Cancian said. “It's not that it can't be done, but you know, I think there are structures that would be better for accomplishing what it is they want, which is the more rapid development of drone capabilities.”

Cancian has argued that a model more like the Missile Defense Agency, a three-star command with its own significant budget, is probably better suited to what Hegseth would like to accomplish with AUTOWARCOM.

“The model of, ‘they develop a technology, develop a system, and then hand it off to the services’—that makes a lot of sense,” he said. “It would be a very bad idea to have this command take over drone operations for all the services, because those operations need to be very tightly coordinated, very tightly integrated with the operating forces, and having them work for someone far away, and someone separate and centralized, I think, would be a very bad idea.”

Ferrari said it’s more likely that AUTOWARCOM will have responsibility for some training and doctrine associated with the new systems, rather than the actual use of them.

“The responsibility is going to be to pull all of this stuff together, and take all these disparate organizations that are working on this stuff, focus them with money, and then get the stuff in the hands of warfighters, right?” he said. “Because buying it is the easy part. Using it is the hard part.”

Then there is the matter of what the command’s force structure will look like. The day after Hegseth announced AUTOWARCOM, the Army announced it would bring online its own autonomy command promptly. Days later, the service rebranded its Futures and Concepts Command as Futures and Autonomy Command, creating a fully staffed and funded AUTOWARCOM component command with minimal friction.

The Navy and Air Force, when asked about their plans to set up component commands, referred Defense One to the Office of the Secretary of Defense. 

“I think, you know, if they actually did this, they'd create some sort of component command,” Cancian said. “Probably dual-task some existing organization, the way the Army has done.”

The Pentagon is working with the services to “ensure autonomous capabilities are integrated,” a Pentagon official, who was not authorized to speak on the record, told Defense One. 

“The Services support AUTOWARCOM and are taking complementary actions to organize and integrate autonomous capabilities within their respective forces, based on their unique operational requirements, force-development responsibilities, and domain expertise,” the official said.

They pointed to the Navy’s new Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Robotic and Autonomous Systems and said the Air Force is “actively exploring organizational structure elements to enable rapid implementation and training of unmanned systems.”

The official did not directly answer a question about whether Hegseth was inspired to create AUTOWARCOM by pre-existing Army plans, instead reiterating that the service’s announcement followed the secretary’s.

Who will lead it?

Who will lead the new command? The military already has enlisted drone operators,  some junior officers with experience integrating unmanned and autonomous systems into their units, and a handful of senior officers who have been leading larger formations as they have integrated more unmanned capabilities.

“There are a lot of warfighters out there who know what they're doing,” Ferrari said. ”And it's unfortunate, because you’ve got a [Chris] Donahue, or Erik Kurilla, or Randy George, right? So there are three people who could have led that thing. Warfighters.”

Those former Army four-stars—the former head of U.S. European and Africa Command, head of U.S. Central Command, and Army chief of staff, respectively—were forced into retirement over the past year or so.

Kurilla and Donahue weren’t selected for follow-on jobs, despite expectations. George was flat-out asked to leave early, opening an opportunity for Hegseth’s senior military aide, Gen. Chris LaNeve, to take over as Army chief. 

The department will announce leaders when appropriate, the Pentagon official said. A plan of action and milestones is due at the end of this month.

The funding elephant in the room

Earlier this year, the Defense Department asked for $54 billion to fund the Defense Autonomous Warfare Group, which Hegseth has since said would be used to get the new command off the ground. 

But the Trump administration elected to request that sum, along with several other top military priorities, not in the $1 trillion defense budget but in a separate bill to be passed under a process rarely used for Pentagon spending before last year. 

“We’re running fast immediately with the committees to ensure that that reconciliation bill, at a minimum of $350 billion, potentially more, ultimately fills up what this department needs,” the Pentagon official said.

But reconciliation bills are a hard sell, even for Republican members of Congress allied with the Trump administration. As the midterm election threatens to shift the balance of power back to Democrats, extra funding on top of the budget request is not even remotely a done deal. 

“Either the money shows up by Christmas or it ain't coming, because when the new Congress gets seated in January, there is no reconciliation anymore,” Ferrari said. “It's over.”

He said the Pentagon could still stand up the organization, but it won’t have the buying power necessary to meet its mission.

Or, Cancian suggested, they can try to squeeze some acquisition money out of the services.

“And the services are not going to be happy about that,” he said. “You're already going to have to give a whole bunch of people to this new command. They'll be levied for joint billets. To say, ‘All right, we want you to give up a thousand people and X billion dollars for this new thing’—it’ll be very difficult to do.”

Asked whether the Pentagon has a back-up plan to fund AUTOWARCOM, the official reiterated that the department is asking for the $54 billion through reconciliation.

Said Ferrari: “If there's no money, it's an interesting concept, and we can ponder on this thing over the next two or three years, because it's not going to go anywhere fast.”

item.title: Navy’s tech playbook serves as ‘toolkit’ for rest of government
item.description: The U.S. Navy dramatically upped its use of pilot tech programs, shuttered old technology systems and moved into the modern tech arena—and it is sharing its lessons learned from along the way.
item.dc:creator: Frank Konkel and Christian Robles
item.content:encoded:
The IBM Center for the Business of Government and Foundation for American Innovation published a playbook for enterprise IT modernization over the summer based largely on the U.S. Navy’s successful framework for technology acquisition.

“Basically, they observed something we were doing — we were getting a handful of wins on common problems, and other agencies started copying it, and we started sharing what we were doing,” Navy Chief Technology Officer Justin Fanelli said on the sidelines of the SAP Public Sector Summit on Oct. 14 in Washington, D.C.

“They asked us, ‘What are you doing that’s different from other pockets that aren’t moving as fast?’ And essentially, we said, ‘Oh, we have a kit for that because we moved from the world of build-everything-yourself to a fast adopter,’” Fanelli said.

The aforementioned kit—the Navy’s framework for technology acquisition — became the basis for a roundtable discussion that culminated in the playbook. It gives three recommendations to agencies for modernizing technology systems.

The first recommendation is to understand the systems agencies operate and how they communicate with each other. The playbook says IT mapping best occurs by mapping processes, data and finances.

“To do modernization that actually benefits the portfolio, you need to have a picture of that portfolio going in,” Daniel Chenok, executive director of the IBM Center for the Business of Government, told Nextgov/FCW.

The second recommendation is to measure pilots against existing systems they are meant to replace with standardized outcome measures. The Navy picked user time saved or lost, adaptability, cost per user, user experience and operational resilience metrics to assess technology, the report notes.

Fanelli said that prior to 2025, the Navy was only executing a few true technology pilots each year. That year, the Navy increased its pilot use by ten times to about 25, and in 2026 has “dozens and dozens” of ongoing pilots on everything from AI, hosting hardware, edge computing and autonomy functions to nuanced technology like float sensors.

“It’s a pretty wide scope,” Fanelli said.

The department, he said, is now communicating with the same tech terminology and more transparently with each other about ongoing pilot work, reducing duplicative, siloed efforts.

In addition, the Navy has found the private sector to be a willing partner in piloting its commercial technology. Both decisions have allowed the Navy to increase its pilot proclivity without breaking the bank or budget.

“Instead of using only government money to do piloting, there are just way more private sector companies who are using their own funding to do pilots to say, ‘Hey, this is already a pretty mature capability.’ (Then), We only have to fund the last five yards (to score a touchdown),” Fanelli said.

Several pilot programs are now critical to department operations. For example, Project Dynamis was piloted by the Navy and U.S. Marine Corps in September 2025 to close the “sensor-to-shooter” gap. The program now deploys critical software like the Maven Smart System to major commands, including the Marine expeditionary forces, and is the command-and-control program of record for the Marine Corps.

So far, Fanelli said ten pilots have transitioned to enterprise services or programs of record, and there is a queue of more than two dozen potential use cases.

“Those pilots have converted into, in many cases, designated enterprise services or programs of record,” Fanelli said. “So instead of hundreds of competing things that float around forever, we're now converting pilots into higher value and higher-impact enterprise services.”

“That is allowing us to cattle-drive legacy [technology],” Fanelli added, referencing Operation Cattle Drive, the Navy’s strategic initiative to identify, consolidate, and retire redundant, insecure and outdated IT systems.

Operation Cattle Drive demands structured divestments from old and outdated technology, and serves as the impetus for the playbook's third recommendation: to adopt an “acquire while divesting” strategy to ensure agencies do not layer new technology on old systems.

Agencies could meet the strategy by requiring divestment planning in solicitations, incorporating divestment planning in project planning and including retirement milestones in funding plans, the playbook says.

“There’s an old [President Ronald] Reagan quote summarized: ‘The closest thing to life everlasting is being a government program,’” Fanelli said. “How are you actually getting rid of things?”

The playbook builds on recent work from the IBM Center for the Business of Government, including a digital modernization implementation framework and an IT modernization roadmap.

item.title: Are yearlong deployments the Navy’s new normal?
item.description: That's what officials are telling sailors' families in Japan, where two destroyers are slated for 12- and 14-month cruises.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Hlad
item.content:encoded:
When the U.S. Navy destroyer John Finn left home in January, sailors expected to be home in March. Now, after extensions on top of extensions, their families have been told to expect them next March—after a 14-month deployment.

The Mustin, another Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, switched homeports this year, leaving San Diego in February and arriving in Yokosuka, Japan, in March. As the sailors stepped off the ship, they were told they needed to be ready to deploy “tomorrow.”

The Mustin actually left Japan in April for a deployment that was supposed to end in August. Now its crew has been told they will return in April 2027, the spouse of one of the sailors told Defense One.

These marathon deployments—a month or more longer than the carrier Abraham Lincoln’s record-breaking 322 days—may be the new normal for U.S. warships. Last week, a Navy official told families at Yokosuka that all ship deployments and patrols, stateside and overseas, will be 10 to 12 months long for the foreseeable future.

Asked about that statement, a Navy spokesperson told Defense One, “It is U.S. Navy policy not to discuss future operations or movements due to operations security.” 

But last month, Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle said that sailors and their families should expect “longer deployments” until “I can grow the Navy we need.” The service’s battle force currently consists of about 290 warships, down from 295 two years ago but up from about 275 a decade ago.

In recent decades, the Navy has generally kept deployments to six or seven months, although that is not a set-in-stone policy, said Katherine Kuzminski, vice president of studies at the Center for a New American Security. But, she said, “that commitment is being violated now.”

“Certainly, depending on operational needs and demands, I think service members and their families are fully on board with providing—with the requirements that are put on them in ongoing operations,” Kuzminski said. “A potential way that the Navy can mitigate this is actually to just commit to the longer term upfront and be clear with service members and their families.” 

After initial reports of the Lincoln’s woes emerged, some veterans of other services and other conflicts were quick to post online about their own longer deployments. But the issue, Kuzminski said, is not so much the length of the deployment, but the “dissonance between what was said at the beginning and what is happening in actuality.”

That dissonance is particularly pronounced for the John Finn, one of several “forward deployed” guided-missile destroyers based at Yokosuka. While other Navy ships tend to deploy for about six months and then return home for a year, forward-deployed ships typically leave for two or three months at a time, then return to port for two to three months of maintenance before heading back out to sea. Those deployments are designed to keep the ships ready for combat in the region, deter aggression from China, and “maintain a free and open Indo-Pacific.” 

Last year, the John Finn left home in June for a “normal” deployment in the region and returned in early November. But much of the following two months were spent in hasty preparations to return to sea.

“We really only saw him a collective 20 days,” the spouse of a sailor on the ship told Defense One.

In early January, the ship left again, for what was expected to be a deployment of perhaps 45 to 60 days. It headed to the Indian Ocean and was involved in the boarding of a Venezuelan oil tanker before being directed to the Arabian Sea, shortly before Operation Epic Fury began.  

The ship was part of the initial attack on Iran, the spouse said, and they’re “still there.” 

Earlier this month, the sailors were told they would likely not be home until March 2027.

“There’s cars that were left on base that have been stickered to be towed and then to be junked. So there’s sailors that are going to come back and have no cars,” the spouse said. “They left in the winter months, and there’s some sailors that live off base and are single sailors and will have abandoned their entire house, their apartment, for over a year. And when they left in the winter months, when they left everything on heat mode, and then the summer came.” Sailors know “that they’re going to come home and all their stuff will be trashed.”

For families, it’s more than a year without a parent—without any of the planning for a long deployment.

“It’s been absolutely gut-wrenching to my kids,” the spouse said, and there is “next to no mental health support” available on base. The deployment length is “absolutely unheard-of for a destroyer,” she said.

The Finn’s story is extreme—but not unique among Yokosuka-based destroyers. 

Photos posted on the Pentagon’s DVIDS media site show the Rafael Peralta in the Philippine Sea in November, in the South China Sea in December, and back in the Philippine Sea on Jan. 8. Then, instead of returning home, it headed for the Middle East in April, where it remains today. Families have been told not to expect the ship home until April 2027.

The Higgins, which lost power and propulsion for a few hours in the Indo-Pacific in April, continued its deployment after repairs and is currently operating in the Indian Ocean. The Milius left Japan in February and has been in the Middle East since March.

The Mustin left its old homeport of San Diego in February and arrived in Japan in March. Sailors are usually given 30 days to help their families move and settle in for a homeport shift, particularly when the move is to a foreign country, and the majority of the families had waited until the ship arrived to make the move. But “the moment they pulled in, my husband stepped off the ship, and he goes, ‘We have to be prepared to leave tomorrow,” a Mustin spouse told Defense One.

The ship did stay in its new port for a few weeks because of a sonar problem that required an expert to fly in to fix it, but sailors did not get time off during that time frame because they needed to be ready at a moment’s notice, the spouse said. They left in April with the expectation that they would return in August and then go out again over the holidays before monthslong scheduled maintenance beginning in February.

But when August came, the ship’s commander told the sailors they would be out for “about another month,” the spouse said. A few weeks ago, they were told they wouldn’t be home until April 2027.

The situation is all the more frustrating for sailors and families because the ship has spent virtually the entire deployment in the Indian Ocean as “backup.”

“They’re not in the blockade, they’re like the next in line, just out there waiting,” she said.

The distinction means that the Mustin sailors don’t get combat pay or benefits.

“I know they feel forgotten about,” she said.

The John Finn spouse said it has been frustrating for families and sailors to read all the media coverage of the Lincoln’s long deployment, while knowing that other ships supporting her were “left behind.”

“I can do a long deployment,” she said. “The problem with this is that there is no answer as to when this will be over. … Why are we not rotating ships? And then why are we there? Why are you sending home stateside ships before your forward deployed ships?”

In response to questions about why the ships have not been replaced, a Navy spokesperson said, “The Department takes a thoughtful and deliberate approach to global force management, continually balancing immediate operational requirements against risks across theaters.” 

If longer deployments increasingly become the norm, Kuzminski said, it’s important that the Navy be upfront with sailors and their families about what to expect. 

But the situation highlights another problem: The Navy doesn’t have a confirmed civilian secretary, “a person who is fundamentally the accountability to Congress on how things are working,” she said.

Without a Navy secretary, she said, it’s hard to answer the big questions: “Is this the new normal? How are you handling that? How are we preparing sailors for that? How are we preparing their families for that? How are we preparing our ships for that?”

item.title: Defense Business Brief: A little bit of MOSA; Netherlands-U.S. industry days, and more
item.dc:creator: Lauren C. Williams
item.content:encoded:
Military buyers want to move quickly, which can mean companies need to add new tech to vehicles after they’re built. Now, Oshkosh Defense is building a dedicated center to test those modifications. 

“We call it the Vehicle Integration Center. It allows us to prove out and test conformance in the real world. So that's work that we'll be doing in ‘27,” Logan Jones, Oshkosh Defense’s chief growth officer, told Defense One. 

“The question of ‘does it work?’ is still left way too late in the process,” Jones said. “We want to shorten that from like a year and a half to weeks.”

While the focus is on their own offerings, Jones said the integration center could help other combat vehicle makers test their products.

“The primes are going to be interested,” he said. “The signal in the market that we've seen is we would be taking risk out of their program—and that's what they want. They want speed, and they want low risk, so they can predict when it'll be available.”

The aim, at least in part, is to make the process easier on engineers. For example: Let's say you're an engineer doing the counter-UAS solution. You said ‘I'm going to bolt it on.’ You need to know where the mounting locations are,” Jones said, noting that information is usually in an interface control document, or ICD. “We don't make that easy today…But in the future, it should be a turnkey system” where the ICDs are easy to access. 

Oshkosh is cleaning up ICDs and aims to start work at the center early next year.

Welcome

You’ve reached the Defense Business Brief, where we dig into what the Pentagon buys, who they’re buying from, and why. Send along your tips, feedback, and song recommendations to lwilliams@defenseone.com. Check out the Defense Business Brief archive here, and tell your friends to subscribe!

How the Dutch are rethinking weapons buying. The U.S. isn’t the only nation with procurement woes. The Netherlands has spent recent years trying to revamp its acquisition system, and there’s a push to incentivize manufacturers to stay ready, Derk Boswijk, the minister for arms procurement and personnel, told reporters. 

  • “We can buy 1 million drones, but I know one thing for sure: that weeks from now they are outdated. So we have to come up with a new model, and we are already working on it,” Boswijk said. 
  • That model would have the government pay commercial companies to be on-call, in a way, to produce certain military products during a conflict. 
  • For example, the government could pay an automaker to make drones. “In the meantime, you do the research, you build prototypes,” and order supplies, he said. But when a conflict “breaks loose, they put everything aside and…produce the drones instead of the automobiles.”
  • Boswijk spoke with a sense of urgency to try something different: “The most dangerous thing we can do is play [it] safe …I have to take [risks] because otherwise, when I want to have 100 percent certainty, then I know for sure…it will be too late.”
  • A bit more: Two U.S. companies inked deals during last week’s annual Netherlands-U.S. defense industry event: Bell Textron and Lockheed Martin.
  • Bell had two memorandums of understanding: one with PhotonFirst to explore the use of fiber optic sensing to monitor aircrafts’ structural health and another with the Netherlands Industries for Defense & Securities. 
  • The latter agreement is “really to facilitate relationships on how they can help us and find other partners in the Netherlands,” Robbie Yarbrough, director of international industrial cooperation at Bell Textron, told Defense One. “And next month, we'll be signing a few more MOUs, and we're really looking for research and technology.”
  • Lockheed Martin Skunk Works signed an agreement with the Royal Netherlands Aerospace Center in support of the Dutch air force. The deal expands an existing agreement and broadens industrial base access. 

MQ-25 Stingray progress report. The Navy successfully synced the aircraft carrier USS Ronald Reagan to an unmanned tanker located more than 2,100 miles away via satellite as part of a series of preliminary sea-trial tests “to validate procedures, networks and interfaces,” the service said in a news release. 

  • “Once the satellite link was up, air vehicle pilots aboard USS Ronald Reagan (CVN 76) connected to the MQ-25A air vehicle on the ground in Mascoutah, Illinois,” the Navy told Defense One via email. “Using the MD-5C [unmanned air command and control station] aboard the ship, the AVPs gave the air vehicle multiple commands to exercise various subsystems of the aircraft and verify an established connection.”
  • Context: The Navy has made several strides with its drone tanker program this year. The program is considered to be a “pathfinder” effort designed to relieve F/A-18E/F aircraft from their refueling duties to focus more on strike missions. 
  • Related: The Navy awarded Applied Intuition a contract for AI data infrastructure “across the manned and unmanned fleet,” the company announced. The service previously awarded the company a contract for its data engine solution and will build on that.  
  • “Its Intelligent Perception System will be the first fleet-scale capability deployed, starting with five Arleigh Burke-class destroyers under the Portfolio Acquisition Executive Robotic and Autonomous Systems and PAE Mission Systems initiative,” the company said in a news release. 

Making moves + other news

  • BAE Systems bought about 13 acres in Weld County, Colorado, to expand manufacturing related to space-based hardware and sensor systems.
  • The Army expanded its enterprise contract with Striveworks tenfold to $700 million for fullstack AI solutions. The company also has a separate $200 million Army contract for the service’s Next Generation Command and Control program.   
  • Electra plans to demonstrate its hybrid-electric Ultra Short aircraft in Lower Manhattan on Friday. The event is expected to be the “first-ever landing at the heliport by a fixed-wing aircraft without vertical takeoff capability,” the company said in a news release.
  • The National Armamfents Consortium added new members and elected James Miller of the Practical Energetics Research as its executive chairman. 
  • The Pentagon awarded Nikon Advanced Manufacturing a contract with an unspecified amount for “customized additive manufacturing systems targeted for production of Tomahawk Land Attack Missile mid-bodies, and other similar potential applications,” the company said in a news release. The award is part of the Defense Department’s Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment program.  
  • Defense tech firms like Palantir are getting more attention—from Wikipedia editors, the Guardian reported. Fun fact: Once upon a time, I wrote “a long article” about that very unique world.
